title: Tav Prasad Savaiye
hook: ten verses saying that kings, armies and rituals are nothing without love

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jaap Sahib, Guru Gobind Singh's galloping praise. Your line was the rhythm of praise. What beat reminded you of it? Today, the same Guru, in a very different mood. Day one hundred thirty-one.

Scroll any feed for five minutes and you'll see what the world calls impressive. The mansion. The supercar. The influencer at the temple at sunrise, perfectly lit. Followers in the millions. Now imagine a poet who had seen the equivalent of all that in his own day, the richest kings, the biggest armies, the most admired ascetics and pilgrims, and wrote ten short poems that keep turning back to the same thought. All of it, he says, is worth nothing, without one thing.
screen: `THE MANSION, THE SUPERCAR.` → `THE PERFECT HOLY PHOTO.` → `ALL OF IT, WORTH NOTHING.`

segments.voice: The poems are the Tav Prasad Savaiye, the third bani of the Sikh morning. Tav prasad means by your grace. Savaiya is the name of the poetic form: a four-line verse with long, flowing lines, beautiful to recite. These ten come from Guru Gobind Singh's Akal Ustat, the praise of the Timeless, in the Dasam Granth. Each verse is a parade. In paraphrase: I have seen the pure ascetics, the yogis, the celibates, crowds of them. I have seen mighty kings riding elephants with golden trappings, great horses, armies without number, emperors who conquered the earth. I have seen pilgrims bathing at every holy river, people fasting, people performing every ritual. And then, as the verses close, the turn. Without the Lord, without love, none of it counts for anything. And the famous line, again in paraphrase: I tell the truth, listen, everyone: only those who loved found the Lord. Notice who is saying this. Guru Gobind Singh was himself a leader of armies, who knew horses and weapons and power from the inside. He's not sneering at kings from the outside. He's saying, as someone who knew that world: it isn't the thing. Neither is outward religion, done for show. The savaiyas are gentle with no one's pride, including the pride of the pious. What remains after the parade passes? Love. That's why these ten verses sit in the morning. Before the day starts measuring you by what you own or how you look, the savaiyas measure differently.
screen: `TAV PRASAD — BY YOUR GRACE.` · `A PARADE OF KINGS AND HOLY MEN.` · `ONLY THOSE WHO LOVED FOUND GOD.` · `A LEADER OF ARMIES SAYS IT.` · then, large: `WITHOUT LOVE, NOTHING.`

segments.voice: Listen to one savaiya. If you can, play a recording of Tav Prasad Savaiye and listen to just the first verse, about a minute. Notice the long, rolling lines. If you can't play one, try this instead: think of one thing you've been proud of lately, a promotion, a purchase, a good photo. Hold it for a moment. Then ask the savaiyas' question: was there love in it? No judgment. Just the question. The bell holds the time.
Savaiya. A four-line verse with long, flowing lines. Guru Gobind Singh's ten savaiyas keep returning to one thought: without love, nothing.
Your line: without love, nothing. Today, when something impressive crosses your screen, ask the savaiya's question: where's the love in it? Day one hundred thirty-one.

howItsDone: The ten Tav Prasad Savaiye, from Guru Gobind Singh's Akal Ustat, are recited every morning in Nitnem after Jaap Sahib, and are among the five banis of the Amrit ceremony.

original.note: Gurmukhi: savaiya, a four-line verse form with long lines.

trapdoor: what you thought: ten more morning prayers.
what it means: ten verses that parade kings, armies and rituals past, and say none of it counts without love.
what a scholar hears: savaiyas 21 to 30 of Guru Gobind Singh's Akal Ustat, in the Dasam Granth, each turning at its close to the Lord, one naming love outright.

sources.ref: Dasam Granth, Akal Ustat, savaiyas 21–30 (Tav Prasad Savaiye)

notes: Tav Prasad Savaiye as Akal Ustat verses 21–30: commonly given numbering. Confirm.

The refrain 'saach kahon sun leho sabhai jin prem kio tin hi prabh paaio' paraphrased; it closes the first savaiya (verse 29 in some numbering). Confirm placement. Each savaiya's closing line turns on the Lord's grace or name; 'without the Lord, without love' summarizes. Confirm.
Gurmukhi spelling of savaiya varies (ਸਵੱਯਾ / ਸਵੈਯਾ); please confirm the preferred spelling.
Authorship debates about parts of the Dasam Granth not raised; these savaiyas are part of Nitnem and the Amrit ceremony.

Reviewer edit: the draft said all ten verses 'end the same way' / 'end in one refrain'. Softened to 'keep turning back to the same thought', since the prem line closes only one savaiya and the others close on the Lord's name or grace. Hook's 'holiest-looking holy men' changed to 'the most admired ascetics and pilgrims' to avoid a sneering tone toward other traditions' ascetics. Confirm.
